intro: NASA's SPHEREx telescope photographs the whole sky again and again. Stars stay put. Asteroids, comets and maybe a hidden planet move. Watch two real scans flicker and tap anything that jumps.
verdictConfirmedTxt: A known object's orbit puts it at both of these positions at these times, and the light is really there.
verdictPlantedTxt: The game added this dot to real images, so we know the answer. It says nothing about the real sky.
verdictNoneTxt: {n} known objects were in this field, all too faint to see in these images.
evidenceGone: Light gone from the old spot
evidenceGoneValue: at least {n}%, which a star that only changes brightness wouldn't do
evidenceSourceReal: NASA SPHEREx {release} via IRSA. Object positions: IMCCE SkyBoT
evidenceSourceSim: Real SPHEREx {release} images via IRSA, with a dot added by the game
evidenceLimitReal: These are archive images, not a live feed. This checks against known objects, so it isn't a new discovery, and the two images were taken at different wavelengths.
evidenceLimitSim: Real objects are often fainter and harder to separate from stars than this.
roundsFailed: The cases didn't load. Check your connection and try again. The Sky Explorer and Practice may still work.
explorePitch: Enter any Right Ascension and Declination and watch real SPHEREx images of that patch play like a little video.
explorerIntro: Real SPHEREx images of any patch of sky, played in time order. Anything that shifts between frames has moved.
coordsError: Please check the coordinates. Use degrees (133.795, -7.245) or forms like 08h55m10.8s and -7d14m42.5s.
explorerIdle: Pick a target above or enter coordinates. A larger field or more images takes longer to load.
searching: Asking NASA's archive which images contain this position…
loadingFrames: Loading images from NASA's archive: {n} of {total}. A patch nobody has opened yet can take a minute or two.
loadedFrames: Showing {n} images, out of {here} on this detector and {all} from all six.
noCoverage: No images on this detector yet ({n} on the others). Try another detector.
archiveFailed: NASA's archive didn't answer. Press “Show this sky” to try again.
searchPartial: One data release didn't answer, so some images may be missing.
hint_exposure: Each image sees a slightly different wavelength, so a star's brightness can flicker. A real mover changes position.
hint_visit: Images from each six-month visit are combined. This hides faint flicker and shows slow movers across the whole survey.
hint_add: All loaded images combined, which shows fainter things. A moving object spreads out or disappears here.
hint_subtract: Stars mostly cancel out. A mover leaves one bright spot and one dark spot. Leftovers around bright stars aren't movers.
overlay_expected: Where it should be on this date
catalogFailed: That catalog didn't load. Try again.
pinHint: Tap the image to read its position, contamination flags and brightness at that point.
noFlux: No usable measurement at this point.
chartNote_spectrum: Measured live from the images here. They were taken at different times, so a variable or moving object will scatter.
chartNote_time: Each image here also has a slightly different wavelength, so not every change is a real change in brightness.
chartNote_saturated: This star is too bright for the detector at its core (the black centre in the image), so these numbers come from its outer glow. They show changes, not its true brightness.
story: In 1930 Clyde Tombaugh was hunting for a “Planet X”, flipping between two photographic plates until one dot jumped. That dot was Pluto. You're using the same trick on SPHEREx.
guideAsteroidTxt: A rocky body, usually between Mars and Jupiter. It's close by, so it can jump a long way in less than a day.
guideDwarfTxt: A small world far beyond Neptune. It crawls: Makemake needs days to move as far as an asteroid does in hours.
guidePlanetXTxt: A predicted planet far beyond Neptune that nobody has seen. It may not exist, and it would be too faint and too slow for SPHEREx to catch.
diffTxt: One scan subtracted from the other. Most of each star cancels out, and any leftovers come from imperfect subtraction. A mover leaves one bright spot and one dark spot.
challengeNote: Challenge mixes real and simulated rounds, 8 in a shuffled order.
loadError: The scans didn't load. Check your connection and reload the page.
hint: Tap the dot that jumps between Scan A and Scan B.
hintMore: {n} more mover to find in this field.
miss: Not a known mover. It could be a star that changed brightness, a cosmic ray, or something new.
noneRightTxt: No known mover is bright enough to see here. Ruling out patches of sky like this is how the Planet X search narrows down.
noneWrongTxt: There was a mover in this field. It's circled now.
badgeSim: Simulated object on a real SPHEREx image
simTxt: The game planted this dot to train your eye. Real asteroids look just like it.
skyTxt: Every empty patch you check narrows where a Planet X could hide. SPHEREx maps the whole sky, about 41,000 square degrees, every six months.
credit: SPHEREx images: NASA/JPL-Caltech via NASA/IPAC IRSA. Asteroid positions: IMCCE SkyBoT and JPL Horizons. Facts: JPL Small-Body Database.
